blocks.text: Prompt caching lets a model provider reuse the processing already done on a repeated, stable portion of a prompt, a long system prompt or a large piece of context, avoiding the cost and latency of reprocessing those same tokens from scratch on every single call.

This topic covers the problem of repeatedly reprocessing an identical prefix, how provider-level caching addresses it, structuring a prompt to actually maximize cache hits, and how this differs from prompt compression, covered in the previous topic.
1. What Prompt Caching Means

blocks.alt: Building on prompt compression, prompt caching reuses already processed prefixes

blocks.text: Prompt caching is a feature many model providers offer that stores the internal processing result for a portion of a prompt, so that when the exact same portion appears again in a later call, the provider can reuse that stored result instead of processing it again from scratch.
2. The Stable Prefix Problem

blocks.alt: The same long prefix sent every call gets reprocessed from scratch every single time without caching

blocks.text: A production application often sends the same long system prompt, or the same large reference document, at the start of every single call, with only a small variable portion, the actual user question, genuinely changing, without caching, that entire stable prefix gets fully reprocessed on every call, an obviously wasteful repetition.
3. Stable Prefix vs Variable Suffix

blocks.alt: A stable prefix, the system prompt or long context, is distinguished from a variable suffix, the actual user question

blocks.text: Prompt caching works by distinguishing the part of a prompt that stays genuinely identical across calls, the stable prefix, from the part that actually changes, the variable suffix, this connects directly to the template-based prompting concept covered in an earlier module, the fixed template portion is exactly the caching candidate.

code.content:
# Stable prefix, sent unchanged on every call
system_prompt = "... a long, detailed set of instructions ..."

# Variable suffix, changes with every call
user_question = get_current_user_question()

blocks.text: 4. How Caching Works, Provider Side

blocks.alt: The first call processes and caches the prefix, later calls reuse the cached prefix

blocks.text: The first call including a given stable prefix processes it fully and the provider stores, or caches, that processing result, subsequent calls including that exact same prefix can reuse the cached result rather than reprocessing it, this is covered in more concrete, provider-specific detail in the later Anthropic APIs and OpenAI APIs modules.
5. Cost and Latency Savings

blocks.alt: Without caching, full cost applies every call, with caching, cost is reduced on a cache hit

blocks.text: A cache hit, a call that successfully reuses a previously cached prefix, is typically both cheaper and faster than fully reprocessing that same content again, for an application sending a large stable prefix on every call, this can produce a genuinely significant cost and latency reduction at scale.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Scenario","Effect"],"rows":[["No caching","Full processing cost on every single call"],["Cache hit on a repeated stable prefix","Reduced cost and latency for that portion"]]}

blocks.text: 6. Cache Invalidation

blocks.alt: When the cached prefix content changes, the cache gets invalidated and reprocessed fresh

blocks.text: A cache only helps when the prefix is genuinely identical, even a small change to the supposedly stable prefix, an updated instruction, a slightly modified reference document, invalidates the cache for that content, causing it to be reprocessed fresh, keeping a truly stable prefix genuinely unchanged is what makes caching actually effective.

blocks.title: This is a real practical discipline worth building into a workflow
blocks.content: Frequently tweaking a system prompt that is meant to be a cached stable prefix undermines the caching benefit entirely, treating that prefix as genuinely stable, changed deliberately and infrequently, keeps the cache actually working.

blocks.text: 7. Structuring a Prompt to Maximize Cache Hits

blocks.alt: Stable content placed first and variable content placed last maximizes cache hits

blocks.text: Placing the stable, cacheable content at the very beginning of a prompt, and the variable, changing content at the end, is the structural pattern that lets a provider cache system recognize and reuse the stable portion consistently, mixing stable and variable content together defeats this benefit.
8. Prompt Caching vs Prompt Compression

These two optimization techniques are complementary rather than competing, compression, covered in the previous topic, reduces how many tokens a prompt contains in the first place, caching reduces the cost of reprocessing tokens that are already there but repeated across calls, a well optimized high volume prompt often benefits from both.
9. When Caching Provides the Biggest Win

Caching earns its biggest win specifically for applications with a large, genuinely stable prefix, a long system prompt, an extensive reference document, reused across a high volume of calls, for a prompt with little stable content or run only occasionally, the caching benefit is much smaller.
Worked Example

A team building a document analysis tool sends the same lengthy reference document, several thousand tokens, as context on every single call, along with a short, varying user question, without caching, that reference document gets fully reprocessed on every call.

Restructuring the prompt to place the stable reference document first and the variable question last, and enabling provider-level caching, produces a meaningful reduction in both cost and response latency for the large majority of calls that hit the cache, since the expensive part of the prompt no longer needs full reprocessing every single time.
Common Mistakes

items: Placing variable content before stable content, preventing the provider from recognizing and caching the stable portion
Frequently modifying a prefix meant to be a stable, cached portion, repeatedly invalidating the cache
Not measuring actual cost and latency before and after enabling caching to confirm the expected benefit
Applying caching to a prompt with little genuinely stable, repeated content, where the benefit is minimal

blocks.text: Practice

Take a prompt you send repeatedly with a large stable portion and a small variable portion, restructure it to place the stable content first, and if your provider supports prompt caching, measure the cost and latency difference between a cache miss and a cache hit.
Key Takeaway

Prompt caching lets a provider reuse the processing already done on a stable, repeated prompt prefix, saving cost and latency on subsequent calls, and it works best when a prompt is deliberately structured with stable content first and variable content last, and when that stable portion genuinely stays unchanged across calls rather than being modified frequently.
